session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: I will frame these participants as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — the places they go, the food they eat, the company they keep — rather than as representatives of a gender category or a research subject. The collective identity is grounded in the concrete and the personal: their actual habits, preferences, and experiences. I will avoid academic or activist language entirely, keeping the register conversational and low-stakes.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): This is the most sensitive and socially loaded area. Men in this age group may produce highly rehearsed or defensively dismissive responses ('I just eat what I want'). Behavioural grounding and concrete example-seeking will be essential. Consensus risk is high — the group may rapidly converge on a shared 'gender doesn't matter' position that forecloses richer material.

Plant-based eating acceptability (Sections 4 and 5): Social desirability works in two directions here — some participants may perform open-mindedness they don't feel; others may perform resistance they don't entirely hold. Both require probing for specific past moments rather than general opinions. The masculinity–meat association literature suggests this group may hold implicit links that direct questioning won't surface.

Social context of food choice (Section 2): This section establishes baseline decision-making patterns that will anchor later gender and plant-based probes. If this section is too thin, later probes will lack purchase. Need to push for specificity — meals, occasions, companions — not abstract rules.

Male friendship and place (Section 1): Ostensibly light, but it establishes relational trust and often surfaces incidental data about food, alcohol, and social ritual that is analytically significant later. Worth a light follow-up probe if something rich appears, but should not be exhausted.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Fletcher (64, rural Scotland) may bring a distinctly regional and outdoors-inflected perspective on food and masculinity — farming, game, local produce are plausible reference points. Rural Scottish male norms around food and sociality may differ from the suburban English majority of this group. Worth watching for whether he self-identifies as different or aligns with the group.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Potential outlier voice — if he feels culturally distant from the others, he may disengage. Warm engagement early on will help.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Keith (72, suburban North West) — oldest member by cohort alongside Patrick and Toby. May hold more traditional food attitudes aligned with postwar British working-class or lower-middle-class norms. Could be a strong voice on 'proper meals' and meat-centredness, or conversely a surprising pragmatist. Watch for dominance tendencies in older male group dynamics.

Patrick (73, suburban South East) — South East suburban context may index slightly more exposure to food trends, including plant-based options, than the other participants. At 73 the oldest, may be reflective and measured in tone. Could serve as a reference point for health-motivated food changes given age.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Age may raise health salience — watch for whether he foregrounds health as his primary food frame, which could shape his responses to plant-based sections.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Toby (68, rural South West) — rural South West context suggests possible smallholder, farming, or food-production adjacency. May have strong views on provenance, 'natural' food, and traditional rural masculinity. Could be an interesting counterpoint to plant-based framing if he associates it with urban or progressive culture.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Possible source of strong opinions on plant-based eating — worth watching for early signals of entrenchment or openness.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability on gender: Men in this age cohort may reflexively deny that gender shapes their food choices, either from genuine belief or from not wanting to appear old-fashioned. Plan behavioural grounding in Section 3 — ask for specific meal occasions, social settings, or moments of hesitation rather than abstract attitudes.

Premature consensus on plant-based rejection: This group profile makes early, firm collective dismissal of plant-based eating a likely scenario. Have a sharpening or hypothetical move ready (e.g. a health scenario, a cost scenario, or a practical accessibility probe) to force differentiation.

Polite agreement culture in older male groups: Men of this age in group settings may default to agreeable, non-confrontational responses, particularly with strangers. Watch for thin agreement and be ready to use invite_dissent before consensus hardens.

Topic may activate identity threat: Questions about gendered food norms can feel implicitly accusatory for some participants (as if the question implies they should eat differently). Frame all gender-related questions as descriptive and curious, never normative.

Homogeneous age and gender profile: All four participants are men aged 64–73. This reduces natural diversity and increases consensus risk throughout. Will need to work harder to surface intra-group differences.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1: Light touch. Let participants warm up, establish rapport with each other, and settle into the format. Only probe in the intro or context sections if something genuinely rich appears. Section 2: Moderate directivity — push for specific meals, occasions, and decision moments rather than accepting abstract rules. This builds the behavioural vocabulary for later sections. Sections 3–5: Maximum directivity within the philosophical contract. Use behavioural grounding, contradiction-surfacing, and dissent-inviting actively. These sections carry the research and are where thin, socially performed answers are most likely. Section 6: Very light — a brief, warm close. Do not reopen topics unless a participant volunteers something significant.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) are weighted most heavily as they carry the core research questions. Context sections (1, 2) are weighted moderately — Section 2 slightly more because it establishes the behavioural baseline for later probing. Intro and closing are minimal. The three main topic sections together receive roughly 60% of the total word budget.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was purely introductory — participants oriented themselves to the format, geography, and group dynamic rather than engaging with substantive themes. The dominant tone was reassurance: more experienced participants (Toby, Fletcher) normalised the focus group setting for newcomers (Keith, Patrick). An implicit value around authenticity — saying what you actually think rather than what's expected — emerged organically and was reinforced by the moderator as a framing principle before the first substantive question.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The approach here was minimal intervention: let the group self-organise through introductions and allow natural rapport-building before directing attention to the first topic. Toby and Fletcher's unprompted reassurances to Keith and Patrick did the settling work more effectively than moderator guidance could have. Closing the section by echoing Fletcher's authenticity point and pivoting cleanly to the first question worked as a light bridge — though with only four participants, no quieter voices needed drawing out yet.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on how geography shapes the texture and intentionality of male socialising. A productive tension emerged between rural participants' 'deliberate' sociality — distance forcing commitment and depth — and suburban casualness. Across all contexts, task-based socialising (fixing, building, helping) surfaced as a distinct and valued mode: conversation as by-product of shared work rather than its purpose. Fletcher's implicit claim that effort and mutual usefulness deepen friendship went largely unchallenged.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main intervention was drawing Patrick in after he'd stayed quiet through an extended Fletcher-Toby-Keith exchange. The timing was right — the rural/suburban contrast had crystallised enough for Patrick's middling position to add genuine texture rather than just echo. The section closed itself naturally, so the pivot to food felt clean rather than forced. No strong tensions were left unresolved, though Fletcher's depth-versus-casualness provocation could have been pushed harder.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the practical logic of food provisioning in retirement — using what's available, avoiding waste, adapting to reduced appetite — with geography (rural scarcity) and life-stage (more time at home) operating as reinforcing pressures. Beneath the practical surface, a consistent domestic labour pattern emerged: wives hold the 'mental load' of food planning while husbands describe their own involvement as incidental. This was stated without friction or critical distance by all three participants.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: Keith had been absent from this exchange — Patrick and Toby converged rapidly into mutual agreement, risking a two-person echo chamber. Drawing Fletcher in mid-section was the right call and confirmed rather than complicated the emerging pattern, which itself became useful data. The section closed with a direct pivot to gender and food, capitalising on the unexamined domestic-labour thread. The risk is that the earlier convergence went too unchallenged — the wife-as-planner framing deserved a light probe before moving on.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section refined the domestic-labour pattern from the previous section: gender shapes not passivity toward food but the 'mental load' of longer-view planning — knowing what's in the cupboard, what's going off, what to buy. All four participants distinguished this from the cooking moment itself, which felt gender-neutral and skill-based. Retirement was consistently cited as shifting men toward more active cooking without transferring the planning role. Toby's reframe — habituated roles rather than masculinity per se — introduced a mild complication that went largely unresolved.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section opened with Fletcher's framing, which risked consensus too quickly. Drawing Keith in produced genuine pushback and sharpened a useful cooking/planning distinction that structured the rest of the exchange. Routing Patrick and Toby through that distinction rather than starting fresh worked efficiently. The section closed naturally, so the pivot to plant-based hypothetical felt clean. The main missed opportunity: Toby's 'she's just better at it' naturalisation deserved a light probe rather than being folded into the transition.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section used a plant-based hypothetical to surface three interlocking themes: geographic constraint as a genuine multiplier of dietary change difficulty; the domestic labour question from earlier sections made explicit — whether it is fair, not just possible, to load new complexity onto whoever already carries the planning burden; and retirement as a structural variable that either enables or forecloses men's capacity to engage with that burden themselves.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: Three moderator interventions were needed to bring Toby and Patrick into what had become a sustained Fletcher-Keith exchange. The timing was right — Fletcher's fairness reframe at turn 28 gave Patrick something to push back against, producing the section's most generative moment. Toby remained harder to draw out and ultimately aligned with Fletcher rather than adding texture. The pivot away from logistics toward appeal was a clean close, though Fletcher's 'is it fair' thread could have been held open slightly longer.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section reframed the barriers to plant-based eating around perceived versus actual complexity. The dominant theme was experiential unfamiliarity as the real obstacle — not logistics or planning, but never having tried something and therefore overestimating its difficulty. Toby's lentil stew example introduced a distinct mechanism: quiet, unremarkable exposure ('just making the tea') as more effective than persuasion or planning frameworks. This shifted the section's register from structural constraint toward the social conditions of first encounter.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The pivot from Patrick's 'fiddly' observation to a group probe worked — it gave Toby room to introduce lived counter-evidence, which Patrick then genuinely engaged with rather than deflecting. The two-person exchange that followed was generative and self-sustaining, so holding back was the right call. Fletcher and Keith went unheard in this section, which is a mild gap, though the closing invitation to final remarks opens that space. No strong moderator errors, but Fletcher's earlier 'fairness' thread was quietly abandoned.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section returned Fletcher's 'fairness' thread to the foreground as a closing statement rather than a new theme. Its function was more consolidating than generative: Fletcher synthesised the planning-load argument across the session's earlier sections, explicitly linking rural constraint, domestic labour, and the limits of experiential exposure as a change mechanism. The section added little new content but gave the fairness framing a conclusive register it had previously lacked.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator's move was to let Fletcher's unsolicited synthesis land without interruption, then use it as a natural session close rather than reopening threads. Framing Fletcher's point as something 'that's run through the whole conversation' retrospectively validated the planning-load theme as a through-line. The open invitation for final remarks was a clean low-pressure close. The risk: Fletcher's monologue went unchallenged and the other three participants were effectively silenced at the section's only moment.

Hi everyone, and welcome — really glad you could all make it today. My name's Alex, and I'll be facilitating our conversation. We've got about 45 minutes together, and it's going to be recorded for research purposes, so just bear that in mind.

The main thing I want to say before we get going is that this is genuinely a conversation — not a quiz, not an interview where I'm looking for particular answers. Whatever you actually think, feel, or do is exactly what's useful here. You might find yourselves agreeing with each other, you might find you see things completely differently — both of those are fine, and honestly both are interesting. If something someone else says connects with your own experience, just jump in. You don't need to wait to be asked.

Okay, let's get started. Let's go around and if everyone could just say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today, that would be great.

Yeah, hi everyone. I'm Keith, I'm from the North West — just outside Manchester actually, in the suburbs. I'm 72, retired now. First time doing one of these focus groups, so I'm not entirely sure what to expect, but I'm happy to be here and have a chat. Seems straightforward enough.

Right, yeah. I'm Patrick, I'm 73, and I'm down in the South East — suburban area. And like Keith here, I'm retired as well, so I know what you mean about not knowing what to expect. Only my second time doing something like this actually, so it's all a bit new to me still. But I'm looking forward to it. Seems like a relaxed sort of thing, so that's good.

Yeah, hi everyone. I'm Toby, 68, from down here in the South West — rural bit actually, nowhere near a town. I've done a few of these groups before so I know the ropes a bit.

Keith, Patrick, honestly there's nothing to worry about. Alex here is right — it's just a chat really. Nobody's testing you on anything. You just say what you think. I found the first one a bit odd, I'll be honest, sitting round with strangers talking into a recorder, but after five minutes you forget about it and it's just normal conversation. So don't stress about it.

Right, yeah, I'm Fletcher. I'm 64, up here in rural Scotland — proper rural, you know, not on anyone's doorstep. I've done a couple of these before as well, so I know what Toby means about it becoming normal after a bit.

I'll be honest, the recording thing still gets to me a wee bit, but you're right, Toby, you forget about it. I think the main thing is just to say what you actually think rather than what you think people want to hear. That's the whole point of it, isn't it?

Good to have some other folk here who've done this before. Makes it feel a bit less formal.

Great, good to have you all here — Fletcher, Toby, Patrick, Keith. And Fletcher, I think that's exactly the spirit of it — just saying what you actually think.

Right, let's get into it. First thing I'd love to hear about is where you actually spend time with your male friends — the places that come to mind. Your favourite spot, wherever that is — pub, club, someone's shed, a park, anywhere. What comes to mind, and what is it about that place that makes it the one?

Well, for me it's mostly the pub, to be honest. There's one about twenty minutes away — it's nothing fancy, just a proper local. That's where you see the same faces, you know? Folk you've known for years. We'll sit there of an evening, have a pint, a chat. It's reliable, that's the thing. You know who you're going to bump into.

And then there's the football — I go down to watch when I can. That's another one where you're with the same crowd week in, week out.

But if I'm being honest, out where I am, you don't have loads of options for just popping somewhere casual. You've got to make a bit of effort to get anywhere, so when you do go out, you make it count. You're not just wandering down the street to meet someone. It's more deliberate than that, I'd say.

Yeah, that's exactly it, Fletcher. You've hit on something there. Out where I am it's the same — you can't just nip down to the pub round the corner because there isn't one round the corner. So when you do meet up with someone, there's a bit more intention to it, you know? You've actually planned it rather than it just happening.

For me it's either down the local, which is a good fifteen, twenty minutes drive, or honestly a lot of it happens at someone's place. Someone's kitchen or garage. We'll have a cup of tea, work on something, have a chat. That's actually where quite a bit of the socialising happens out here — you end up at a mate's house because you're already going in that direction or you've arranged to help them with something.

The pub's nice when you go, but Fletcher's right — it's more of an event. You get yourself ready for it, make the drive. Not like you can just pop in for half an hour between other things. And that does change how you do it, I reckon. Makes it feel a bit different.

Yeah, that's it exactly. You've got it there, Toby. A lot of my time with folk is actually doing something — I'll go round to help someone fix something on their place, mend a fence, sort out the boiler, whatever it is. And you're having a blether while you're doing it, cup of tea going. That's when you actually have proper conversations, I find.

It's not like you're sitting down thinking, right, now I'm going to socialise. You're just... getting on with something and talking. And honestly, that suits me fine. You get something done and you've had company. Two birds with one stone, you know?

The garage thing Toby mentioned — yeah, that happens too. Folk tinker about with cars or whatever they're working on, and you'll drift over, see what they're up to. It's more natural than just sitting in a pub making conversation. You've got something to focus on besides just talking at each other.

Yeah, well it's a bit different where I am. I mean, I'm suburban, so I've got options, haven't I. There's pubs within walking distance, a couple of them. I'll meet mates down the local — it's just round the corner basically, five minutes walk. That's the main one for us. We just sort of... go when we fancy it, really. Don't have to plan it too much.

But what you're saying about the intention thing, Fletcher — I get that, I do. Out where you are you've got to make more of an effort. We're a bit spoiled, I suppose. We can just say, oh, fancy a pint, and off we go. 

Though I will say, even in the suburbs you do end up at someone's house quite a bit. My mate Dave, he's always got something on the go — bit of DIY, garden work, that sort of thing. I'll pop over, we'll have a cup of tea, help him out with whatever it is. That's the same as what you're describing, Toby. You're doing something and chatting at the same time. That's quite nice, actually. More relaxed than just sitting making small talk.

But yeah, the difference is we've got the pub right there if we want it. We can be a bit more casual about it. Not everything has to be an event.

Right, but see, that's the thing though — being casual about it isn't necessarily better, is it? I mean, you can pop down the pub whenever you fancy, but does that mean you see people deeper, you know what I mean?

When you have to plan it, when you've got to make the effort to drive twenty minutes, you're actually committed to it. You're going to sit there for a couple of hours, have a proper night. You're not just popping in for twenty minutes because you're bored. You've got time to actually talk about things.

And the work thing — what you said about Dave, Keith — that's it. That's where real conversation happens, I think. You're doing something with your hands, you're not just staring at each other across a table trying to fill the silence. The chat just flows naturally because you're focused on the job.

Out here, a lot of your friendships are built that way. You help someone with their place, they help you with yours. There's a purpose to it beyond just passing the time. Maybe that sounds a bit... I don't know, but I reckon there's something in it. You're not just mates who go to the pub, you're actually useful to each other.
Patrick, you've been listening to all of this — does any of it ring true from your end, or does it feel different where you are?

Well, I'm somewhere in between, aren't I really. I've got the pubs nearby like Keith — couple within reasonable walking distance — so I can be a bit casual about it. But I'm not as spoiled for choice as he is, and we're not as isolated as you two are out there.

What strikes me though is what Fletcher's saying about the intention and the depth of it. I think he's onto something. I do find when I'm round at a mate's helping with something — I've got a friend who's always got a project on — that's when you actually have a conversation. You're not just sat there thinking what do we talk about next. It just happens naturally while you're getting your hands dirty.

But I wouldn't say the pub is shallow, exactly. It depends who you're with and how long you've known them. With the right lads, you can still have a proper chat down the pub. You're just not forced into it the way you are when you're working on something together.

I suppose we get a bit of both down here. That's probably the main difference for me.

That makes sense — a bit of both. Right, we've got a nice spread there: pubs, garages, mates' kitchens, varying degrees of planning depending on where you live. Let's move on to something a bit more everyday. How do you actually decide what to eat — day to day, week to week? What goes into that?

Well, it's changed a lot since I retired, I'll be honest. When I was working, you didn't really think about it much — you'd grab something at lunch, cook something quick in the evening, or you'd already planned ahead because you knew what your week looked like. Now it's different.

I find I've got more time to think about what I'm eating, which sounds like a good thing, but it also means you can be a bit more... I don't know, leisurely about it. Some days I'll think, right, I'll make a proper stew, take my time with it. Other days I can't be bothered and I'll just have beans on toast or something.

What actually drives it for me is what's in the fridge, to be honest. My wife and I, we'll do a shop at the weekend, but then during the week it's just — what haven't we used yet? We don't like waste. So if there's veg that needs eating, that's what you'll have. If there's a bit of meat in there, you'll work round that.

And your appetite changes a bit at our age, doesn't it? You don't need the same amount as you did. So a tin of soup and a sandwich might be lunch, where you'd have wanted something more substantial years ago. That changes what you're buying, what you're planning for.

I'm not one of these meal-planning people with a spreadsheet or anything like that. It's more just practical, day by day.

That's exactly how it works out here too, Patrick. You can't just nip to the shops whenever you fancy, so you've got to be a bit more thoughtful about what you've got in. And yeah, not wasting things — that's a big one.

I find it's the same as what you're saying, really. You plan your big shop, and then during the week you're working with what you've got. If there's potatoes in the cupboard and veg in the fridge, that's what you're having. My wife does most of the cooking, but we both know it's not about having exactly what you fancy — it's about using what's there before it goes off.

And you're right about the appetite thing. You don't need as much as you used to. I'll have a bit of cheese and bread for lunch, maybe some cold meat from a few days before. That does you fine. You're not thinking about three-course meals or anything like that at our age.

I suppose living out here, you get into that habit anyway because you can't be spontaneous about shopping. You've got to think a bit ahead. Makes you less wasteful, I reckon. You're not buying things just because they're there.

Yeah, that's fair enough. Though I'd say with us it's a bit more mixed. My wife does tend to do most of the cooking still, if I'm honest, but since I've retired I'm doing more of it than I used to. When you're at work all day, you just come home and she's got the tea on, don't you. Now I'm around, I'll do a bit more. Nothing fancy, but I'll make a dinner couple of times a week, or I'll prep something if she's going out.

It's one of those things that changes when you retire, I reckon. You've got the time, so you end up doing a bit more around the house generally. Cooking, tidying, whatever. It's not like a big discussion about it — you just sort of slip into it because you're there.

But you're right, Toby, about the planning side of things. That's the practical thing that runs it all. Whether it's one of you cooking or both of you, you've still got to work with what's in the house. You can't be nipping out to Tesco's every other day at our age — that's a waste of time and money. So you plan the shop, you use what you've got, and you move on.

The wife's probably better at remembering what needs eating though, I'll admit that. She's got the head for it. I'm more just — what's for tea tonight — and she'll say, well, we've got that chicken that needs doing, or we need to use those carrots.

Yeah, that's much the same here. My wife does most of the cooking still, but I'm doing more than I used to now that I'm not working. You just fall into it, don't you — you're there, you might as well do something useful.

But what you said about her remembering what needs eating — that's it exactly. She's got that... I don't know what you'd call it, that sense of what's in there and what's going off. I'll open the fridge and I just see a fridge, you know? She'll open it and she knows there's three days' worth of veg that needs using, or the milk's getting near the end. It's just there in her head somehow.

I do the shopping with her most times now, but honestly I could be looking at the same things and not register half of it the way she does. She's the one who knows what we need, what we've got, what's going to work together. I'm more just... carrying the bags, I suppose.

Not that I'm complaining about it or anything. That's just how it's worked out over the years. But it does mean she's got that responsibility, the planning bit. Even if I'm the one cooking on a given night, she's already thought through what that should be. It's a different kind of work, that thinking ahead bit.
Fletcher, I'm curious whether any of this sounds familiar from your end — or whether it works differently for you?

Yeah, it's pretty much the same setup for us, to be honest. My wife does most of the cooking still, and like you say, Toby, she's the one who's got it all in her head — what needs using, what's going off. I couldn't tell you half of what's in the cupboard if you asked me.

Though I do more of the cooking now than I did when I was working, same as Patrick. Just because you're there, you might as well. And out here it's the same thing — you can't just pop to the shops whenever, so you've got to work with what you've got. Big shop at the weekend, then you're using what's there through the week.

The waste thing Toby mentioned — that's real out here. You're not throwing things away because you couldn't be bothered with them. You use what you've got because it costs money to replace it and you can't just nip out. It's practical, that's all.

Don't really think about it much beyond that, to be honest. You eat what's there, you don't go hungry, and you don't waste things. That's the long and short of it for us.

So there's a pretty consistent thread across all of you — working with what's there, not wasting things, and your wife holding that mental picture of the fridge even when you're both involved in the cooking. That's a useful picture to have. I want to shift us onto something a bit different now. I'm curious about whether being a man shapes what you eat — or whether you think it does. Does your gender influence what ends up on your plate?

Well, I'd say yes, it probably does, though maybe not in the way you might think. I mean, I'm not sitting there thinking, oh, that's a woman's food, I won't eat it. It's not that daft.

But I think — at least out where I am — there's an expectation that your wife's doing the cooking, and you're just... eating what she makes. And if you're doing it, you're doing meat and potatoes type stuff, aren't you? That's what comes naturally to you. You're not thinking about making a nice salad or whatever. You want something that fills you up.

And the shopping side of it — like Toby said, he's just carrying the bags. That's probably true for most of us. The woman's doing the planning, the thinking about nutrition, whether you've had enough vegetables, all that. We're just... eating what appears.

I don't think it's a big dramatic thing, but yeah, I reckon being a man probably does shape it. You're less aware of what goes into the planning of it, less interested in it maybe. You just want your dinner. That's the reality of it, I think. Not everyone's the same, but that's how it's been for me anyway.

Fletcher, thanks — that's a clear way of putting it. Does that land with the rest of you? Is that how it feels — that being a man shapes it more in terms of who's thinking about it than what you actually want on the plate?

Well, I'd push back on that a bit, to be honest. I mean, Fletcher's right that my wife does most of the planning and thinking ahead — that's just how it's worked out for us. But I wouldn't say I'm just eating what appears without thinking about it.

Since I retired, I've been doing more of the cooking, like we said. And I'm not just doing meat and potatoes because that's what men eat. I'll make a stir-fry, I'll do a decent curry, whatever.
